Not directly. None of the three retrieved precedents involve a structuring/smurfing pattern like this one (many feeder accounts each sending a single near-CTR-threshold transfer into a hub account, followed by rapid consolidated outflow).

- case_005 is a mule_hub fan-out case (one account paying many counterparties), which is structurally the reverse of this fan-in pattern, and it was ultimately closed after manual review found a legitimate business explanation (P2P marketplace seller). That precedent is only marginally relevant — it's a cautionary example that even suspicious-looking hub activity can have a benign explanation, but the fact pattern (fan-out vs. fan-in, no near-threshold structuring, corroborated legitimate business) doesn't match this case.
- case_007 is round-tripping (circular flows among 5 accounts), a different typology entirely, though it does show that when all playbook criteria for a typology are matched and no legitimate purpose is found, escalation was approved by the human reviewer — a useful process analogy but not a factual match.
- case_013 is a single low-risk transaction between long-tenured accounts, essentially the opposite risk profile of this case (12 accounts, near-threshold amounts, rapid consolidation, single-use feeder accounts).

This case's own evidence is unusually clean for a textbook structuring typology: all four STR criteria (STR-1 through STR-4) are matched — 12 near-threshold inbound transfers within a 33-hour window, followed by a consolidated outbound transfer 7 hours later, with each feeder account used only once. That is a strong, complete match to the structuring playbook itself, but I don't have a prior *case* in the retrieved set with this same fan-in structuring signature to cite as a direct precedent. I'd recommend treating this as a novel/first instance of a fully-matched structuring pattern in the retrieved history, escalating on the strength of the playbook match alone, and not relying on the above precedents as factual analogues — only case_007 offers a loose procedural analogy (full playbook match + no legitimate purpose → escalate/approve).

citations.note: Superficially similar 'many transactions into/out of a hub account' shape, but it's a fan-out mule_hub case that was closed after legitimate business use was confirmed — illustrates a hub pattern can be benign, but does not match this fan-in structuring fact pattern.
Different typology (round-tripping), but shows precedent for escalating when all playbook criteria for a typology are matched and no legitimate purpose is found.

Low-risk single-transaction case with opposite profile (established accounts, income-consistent amount) — confirms this case's profile (many new/short relationships, near-threshold amounts) is not comparable.
